name: Needing movement or fidgeting/stimming aid in focus
description: Concentration improves when the body is moving, such as tapping, pacing, doodling or fidgeting; sitting perfectly still makes it harder to stay on a task.
source: Inspired by Sarver 2015, J Abnorm Child Psychol 43:1219-1232 (hyperactivity as compensatory behaviour in ADHD)

name: Differences in regulating attention
description: Attention is hard to direct on purpose: it drifts away from tasks that matter, gets pulled by other things, or locks onto something without being chosen.
source: Inspired by DSM-5 inattention criteria (APA 2013) and ASRS-v1.1 (Kessler 2005, Psychol Med 35:245-256)

name: Craving novelty
description: Strong pull toward new experiences, topics or stimulation, and discomfort when things stay the same for long.
source: no reference

name: Hyperactivity (physical and/or mental)
description: Feeling restless in the body or having a mind that keeps racing, even when wanting to rest or relax.
source: Adapted from ASRS-v1.1 items 5, 6, 12-14 (Kessler 2005, Psychol Med 35:245-256) and DSM-5

name: Easily bored
description: Quickly losing interest in tasks that are repetitive, slow-paced, too easy or not stimulating enough, and feeling a strong need to move on.
source: Inspired by Farmer & Sundberg 1986, J Pers Assess 50:4-17 (Boredom Proneness Scale)

name: Difficulty with transitions due to challenges with switching focus
description: Stopping one activity and starting another takes real effort, especially when deeply involved, and the change can feel jarring.
source: Inspired by Miyake 2000, Cogn Psychol 41:49-100 (shifting); autism: Leung & Zakzanis 2014, JADD 44:2628-2645

name: Working memory impacted
description: Information held in mind slips away easily, such as instructions, what was about to be said, or the steps of a task.
source: Inspired by Martinussen 2005, J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 44:377-384 (meta-analysis, ADHD)

name: Different perception of time
description: Time feels hard to judge: hours vanish or drag, deadlines feel abstract, and estimating how long things take is often wrong.
source: Inspired by Noreika 2013, Neuropsychologia 51:235-266 (timing deficits in ADHD)

name: Processing speed impacted
description: Taking in information, forming a response or completing routine steps takes noticeably longer than expected, even when the task is well understood.
source: Inspired by Shanahan 2006, J Abnorm Child Psychol 34:584-601 (processing speed deficits in ADHD)

name: Differences in impulse control
description: Acting, speaking or deciding before thinking it through, and finding it hard to pause between an urge and the action.
source: Inspired by Barkley 1997, Psychol Bull 121:65-94 (behavioural inhibition in ADHD)

name: Executive function difficulties
description: Planning, prioritising, organising and finishing tasks is hard even when knowing exactly what has to be done.
source: Inspired by Willcutt 2005, Biol Psychiatry 57:1336-1346 (executive function theory of ADHD, meta-analysis)

name: Interoception differences
description: Internal body signals such as hunger, thirst, tiredness, temperature or needing the bathroom are noticed late, weakly or too strongly.
source: Inspired by Garfinkel 2016, Biol Psychol 114:117-126 (interoception in autism)

name: Stimming
description: Repeating movements, sounds or actions, such as rocking, humming or tapping, that feel natural or needed, regardless of the reason.
source: Inspired by Kapp 2019, Autism 23:1782-1792 (autistic adults' views and experiences of stimming)

name: Sensory differences
description: Sounds, lights, textures, smells, tastes or touch affect the person more or less strongly than they seem to affect others.
source: Inspired by Crane 2009, Autism 13:215-228 (sensory processing in autistic adults)

name: Hyper and/or hypo-awareness of sensory information
description: Noticing sensory details others miss, such as faint sounds or textures, or missing signals others notice easily, such as pain or temperature.
source: Inspired by Robertson & Baron-Cohen 2017, Nat Rev Neurosci 18:671-684 (sensory perception in autism)

name: Soothed/stimulated through repetitive behaviours, movements, sounds and thoughts (stims)
description: Repeating movements, sounds, thoughts or actions calms, comforts or energises, and being stopped from doing it feels uncomfortable.
source: Inspired by Leekam 2011, Psychol Bull 137:562-593 (restricted and repetitive behaviours in autism)

name: Social interactions affected by impulse control and focus differences
description: Conversations are affected by interrupting, losing the thread, answering too fast or drifting while someone else talks.
source: Inspired by ASRS-v1.1 items 9, 16, 18 (Kessler 2005, Psychol Med 35:245-256)

name: Atypical social interactions
description: Social situations feel different from how others seem to experience them: unwritten rules, small talk and group dynamics are puzzling or tiring.
source: Inspired by AQ-50 social skill items 22, 44, 47 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17)

name: Preference for interpersonal connection through interests
description: Bonding with people comes more easily over a shared interest or activity than through general conversation.
source: no reference

name: Differences in verbal and non-verbal communication and interactions
description: Tone, gestures, eye contact, facial expression or conversational timing are interpreted or expressed differently than expected.
source: Inspired by AQ-50 communication items 26, 33, 35 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17)

name: Preference for direct communication
description: Clear, explicit and literal statements are preferred; hints, implications and unspoken expectations are confusing or tiring.
source: no reference

name: Preference for precision in expression
description: Using exact words matters; inaccurate or vague statements bother the person, who often wants to correct or clarify them.
source: no reference

name: Needing time spent in solitude/contemplation
description: Time alone is needed to think, process experiences and recover after interacting with people.
source: Inspired by Long & Averill 2003, J Theory Soc Behav 33:21-44 (benefits of solitude)

name: Needing interpersonal connection through shared interest in complexity
description: Feeling connected requires conversations with depth, where complex ideas can be explored together.
source: no reference

name: Divergent/creative thinking
description: Many different ideas or unusual solutions come easily for a single problem, and conventional approaches feel limiting.
source: Inspired by Guilford 1950, Am Psychol 5:444-454 (divergent thinking); ADHD: White & Shah 2006, Pers Individ Dif 40:1121-1131

name: Tendency toward concrete thinking/difficulty with abstract thinking
description: Thinking stays close to literal, tangible and specific things; abstract ideas and figurative language are harder to grasp.
source: Inspired by Minshew 1997, J Int Neuropsychol Soc 3:303-316 (concept formation and complex reasoning in autism)

name: Pattern recognition
description: Patterns, regularities or inconsistencies in information, objects or behaviour are spotted quickly and often unprompted.
source: Inspired by Mottron 2006, JADD 36:27-43 (enhanced perceptual functioning in autism)

name: Preference for logic and fairness
description: Decisions and rules are expected to be logical and applied equally; inconsistent or arbitrary rules feel wrong.
source: no reference

name: Thinking in systems
description: Situations are understood as interconnected parts with rules and effects on each other, and the whole picture matters before the details.
source: Inspired by Baron-Cohen 2003, Phil Trans R Soc B 358:361-374 (systemizing quotient)

name: Ability to notice details
description: Small details, changes or errors that others overlook are noticed easily.
source: Inspired by Happé & Frith 2006, JADD 36:5-25 (weak central coherence, detail-focused style)

name: Tendency to make connections across domains
description: Ideas from unrelated subjects are naturally linked, and analogies between different fields come up easily.
source: no reference

name: Tendency to predict consequences and foresee problems
description: Likely consequences, risks and problems are anticipated before they are visible to others.
source: no reference

name: Rapid comprehension and/or skip thinking
description: New ideas are grasped quickly, often reaching the conclusion before the explanation is finished or its intermediate steps are given.
source: Inspired by Winner 2000, Am Psychol 55:159-169 (precocity: gifted children master a domain faster)

name: Thinking in metaphor and symbol
description: Ideas are understood and explained through metaphors, symbols, analogies or images rather than plain description.
source: no reference

name: Tendency toward abstract thinking
description: Thinking in concepts, principles and theory comes more naturally than thinking in concrete examples.
source: no reference

name: Fascination with theory
description: Explaining how and why things work in theory is enjoyable in itself, even without a practical use.
source: no reference

name: RSD (Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria)
description: Criticism, rejection or disappointing someone causes sudden and intense emotional pain that feels out of proportion.
source: Inspired by Canu & Carlson 2007, J Atten Disord 10:261-275 (rejection sensitivity in adults with ADHD)

name: Alexithymia (difficulty identifying and naming feelings)
description: Feelings are hard to identify or put into words, and an emotion may only be noticed through its physical effects.
source: Used from Bagby 1994, J Psychosom Res 38:23-32 (TAS-20); autism: Kinnaird 2019, Eur Psychiatry 55:80-89

name: Emotional sensitivity
description: Emotions are felt strongly and deeply, take time to settle, and are hard to dial down once triggered.
source: Inspired by Aron & Aron 1997, J Pers Soc Psychol 73:345-368 (sensory-processing sensitivity)

name: Highly developed morals
description: Strong sense of right and wrong, with intense reactions to unfairness, injustice, hypocrisy or broken principles.
source: Inspired by Silverman 1994, Roeper Rev 17:110-116 (moral sensitivity of gifted children)

name: Early emotional awareness
description: Emotions and other people's feelings were noticed and deeply felt from an early age, earlier than peers.
source: no reference

name: Early concern for and ongoing need to explore existential issues
description: Questions about meaning, death, purpose or fairness of life arose early and remain important to think about.
source: no reference

name: Tendency to hyper-focus on a wide range of interests
description: Becoming completely absorbed for hours in many different subjects or activities, one at a time.
source: Inspired by Ashinoff & Abu-Akel 2021, Psychol Res 85:1-19 (hyperfocus as an attention state)

name: Tendency to hyperfocus on a few interests for an extended period of time
description: Staying absorbed in a small number of subjects for weeks or years, with deep and lasting knowledge.
source: Inspired by Klin 2007, Res Pract Persons Severe Disabil 32:89-100 (circumscribed interests in autism)

name: Interest-driven
description: Effort, energy and attention depend heavily on interest; uninteresting tasks are hard to start or finish.
source: Inspired by Murray, Lesser & Lawson 2005, Autism 9:139-156 (monotropism, interest-based attention)

name: Unique ways of learning
description: Learning works best in a personal way, such as self-directed exploration or understanding principles first, rather than standard methods.
source: Inspired by Winner 2000, Am Psychol 55:159-169 (gifted children march to their own drummer)

name: Intense curiosity
description: Strong drive to ask questions and find out how things work, even with no practical benefit.
source: Inspired by Winner 2000, Am Psychol 55:159-169 (gifted children show a rage to master)

name: Learning in a non-linear manner
description: Learning happens through jumps, big-picture understanding or sudden insight rather than step by step in order.
source: Inspired by Silverman 2002, Upside-Down Brilliance: The Visual-Spatial Learner (book)

name: Needing intellectual stimulation/mental challenges
description: A steady need for mentally challenging activities; without them the person feels restless, bored or flat.
source: no reference

name: Wide range of interests
description: Interest in many different subjects at the same time and a habit of exploring new ones.
source: no reference

name: Ability to respond quickly in crisis situations/emergencies
description: In emergencies or urgent situations, thinking clears and decisions or actions are fast and effective.
source: no reference

name: Asynchronous development
description: Skills develop unevenly: some intellectual, emotional, social or practical abilities are far ahead of others.
source: Used from Silverman 1997, Peabody J Educ 72:36-58 (the construct of asynchronous development)

name: Needing routine, order, and/or clear expectations
description: Predictable routines, order and clear expectations bring comfort and help the person function well.
source: Inspired by Leekam 2011, Psychol Bull 137:562-593 (insistence on sameness in autism)

name: Awareness of and need for complexity
description: Simple or shallow environments and explanations feel unsatisfying; depth and complexity are sought and noticed.
source: no reference

name: Difficulty working out what others think, feel or intend
description: Working out another person's thoughts, feelings or intentions, from their face, their words or their actions, takes deliberate effort and often stays uncertain, even with people the person knows.
source: Adapted from AQ-50 items 20, 31, 36, 42, 45 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17); theory of mind: Baron-Cohen 1985

name: Long stretches of talk on one's own topics
description: In conversation the person talks at length about their own subjects, so others find it hard to join in or say that the same subject keeps returning.
source: Adapted from AQ-50 items 18, 39 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17)

name: Comments meant politely that others take as impolite
description: Words meant as neutral, honest or polite are sometimes taken as rude or hurtful by others, and the person often finds out only afterwards.
source: Adapted from AQ-50 items 7, 48 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17)

name: Drawn more to objects and machines than to people
description: Attention and interest go more strongly to objects, machines or tasks than to people, who feel less engaging than a device or an activity.
source: Adapted from AQ-50 items 1, 13, 15 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17)

name: Fascination with numbers, dates, codes and categories
description: Strong interest in numbers, dates, codes or categories of facts, shown by noticing them, remembering them or collecting information about them.
source: Adapted from AQ-50 items 6, 9, 19, 29, 41, 49 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17)

name: Distress when kept from a strong interest
description: A strong interest that brings upset, irritation or a lasting bad mood when time for it is cut short, interrupted or not available.
source: Adapted from AQ-50 item 16 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17)

name: Anxiety in new or unfamiliar situations
description: New or unfamiliar situations, places or people bring worry and tension before and during them, and familiar settings feel much easier.
source: Adapted from AQ-50 item 46 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17)

name: Faint or difficult mental imagery
description: Picturing a scene, a person or the characters of a story in the mind is hard or gives only a faint image.
source: Adapted from AQ-50 items 3, 8 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17); aphantasia: Zeman 2015, Cortex 73:378-380

name: Preference for facts over fiction and pretend play
description: Fiction, making up stories and pretend play feel less natural or less appealing than factual material and real activities, now or in childhood.
source: Adapted from AQ-50 items 14, 21, 24, 40, 50 (Baron-Cohen 2001, JADD 31:5-17)

name: Misplacing everyday belongings
description: Keys, phone, glasses or papers get put down and forgotten, so time goes into searching for them.
source: Adapted from ASRS-v1.1 item 10 (Kessler 2005, Psychol Med 35:245-256)

name: Careless mistakes in tedious or demanding tasks
description: Unintended slips such as skipped steps, wrong numbers or overlooked details, noticed only later.
source: Adapted from ASRS-v1.1 item 7 (Kessler 2005, Psychol Med 35:245-256)

name: Talking more than intended in social situations
description: Says more than planned, finds it hard to stop once started, and notices later that most of the talking was theirs.
source: Adapted from ASRS-v1.1 item 15 (Kessler 2005, Psychol Med 35:245-256)

name: Difficulty waiting for a turn
description: Waiting is uncomfortable when others go first or things take time, such as queues and group activities.
source: Adapted from ASRS-v1.1 item 17 (Kessler 2005, Psychol Med 35:245-256)

name: Difficulty learning to read in childhood
description: Learning to read at school took more effort, needed extra help, or went less well than it did for classmates.
source: Adapted from ARHQ items 2, 3 and 6 (Lefly & Pennington 2000, J Learn Disabil 33:286-296)

name: Difficulty learning letter and colour names
description: Learning the names of letters or colours as a child was slow or hard, even when the items were seen often.
source: Inspired by Denckla & Rudel 1976, Neuropsychologia 14:471-479, and ARHQ item 5

name: Struggling through school more than classmates
description: Schoolwork was harder than for classmates, with reading-heavy classes difficult, a repeated year considered, or a dislike of school.
source: Adapted from ARHQ items 1, 7, 8 and 15 (Lefly & Pennington 2000, J Learn Disabil 33:286-296)

name: Reading more slowly than peers
description: Reading takes longer than for other people of the same age and education, silently or aloud, and lines are often read again.
source: Adapted from ARHQ item 11; Wolf & Katzir-Cohen 2001, Sci Stud Read 5:211-239

name: Difficulty with spelling
description: Spelling words correctly takes effort, now or since childhood, and words are often checked before writing them.
source: Adapted from ARHQ items 13 and 14; Lefly & Pennington 1991, Ann Dyslexia 41:141-162

name: Reversing letters or numbers
description: Letters or numbers are written or read in the wrong order, as a child or still now, including swaps inside words.
source: Adapted from ARHQ items 4 and 19; Terepocki 2002, J Learn Disabil 35:214-233

name: Difficulty remembering names and numbers
description: Remembering people's names, phone numbers, addresses or dates is hard, even soon after hearing or reading them.
source: Adapted from ARHQ items 16 and 17 (Lefly & Pennington 2000, J Learn Disabil 33:286-296)

name: Dislike of reading
description: Reading is unpleasant, so it is avoided when it is optional and is not chosen as a way to spend free time.
source: Inspired by ARHQ item 9; Mol & Bus 2011, Psychol Bull 137:267-296

name: Reading little for pleasure, work or news
description: Little time goes to reading books, magazines, news or material for work, and weeks can pass without reading for pleasure.
source: Adapted from ARHQ items 10, 12, 20-23; Mol & Bus 2011, Psychol Bull 137:267-296

name: Saving or collecting things that are not needed
description: Things are kept or collected beyond what is needed, throwing them away is hard, and the amount saved starts to get in the way of daily life.
source: Adapted from OCI-R hoarding items 1, 7 and 13 (Foa 2002, Psychol Assess 14:485-496)

name: Checking things repeatedly
description: Doors, windows, drawers, taps and switches are checked again and again, more often than needed, even after they were locked or turned off.
source: Adapted from OCI-R checking items 2, 8 and 14 (Foa 2002, Psychol Assess 14:485-496)

name: Distress when objects are not arranged a certain way
description: Objects need to be arranged in a particular way, and it is upsetting when they are not, or when someone else changes the arrangement.
source: Adapted from OCI-R ordering items 3, 9 and 15 (Foa 2002, Psychol Assess 14:485-496)

name: Counting or repeating numbers out of need
description: A felt need to count while doing things, to repeat certain numbers, or to treat some numbers as good and others as bad.
source: Adapted from OCI-R neutralizing items 4, 10 and 16 (Foa 2002, Psychol Assess 14:485-496)

name: Contamination worries and washing
description: Touching things that others have touched feels hard, and washing or cleaning happens more than needed because of a feeling of being contaminated.
source: Adapted from OCI-R washing items 5, 11 and 17 (Foa 2002, Psychol Assess 14:485-496)

name: Unwanted unpleasant thoughts that are hard to dismiss
description: Unpleasant thoughts come to mind against one's will, and they are hard to control or to get rid of once they are there.
source: Adapted from OCI-R obsessing items 6, 12 and 18 (Foa 2002, Psychol Assess 14:485-496)
